The release then promotes the same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production with approvals and checks at each stage, using Ansible, Python and Shell scripts for multi-node installs, and every environment traces back to one tagged version.
i: Branch policies require a green build and reviewers before merge.
Versioning: semantic version plus build number and commit hash stamped into the artifact.
Environment approvals and checks (business hours, change request id) in Azure DevOps environments.
Post-deploy verification: version check on every node, health endpoints and smoke tests.
Since [2025] most deployments are driven through the CIRT MCP server, which triggers the same releases.
c:
trigger: { branches: { include: [ main, release/* ] } }
stages:
- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: build
    steps:
    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      inputs: { command: test, projects: '**/*Tests.csproj', arguments: '--collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"' }
    - task: SonarQubeAnalyze@6
    - task: PublishPipelineArtifact@1
      inputs: { targetPath: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)', artifact: 'drop' }
f: How do you make sure production gets exactly what was tested?
Build once, promote the same immutable artifact; never rebuild per environment.
What checks run before production?
Approvals by release manager and QA, change request reference, FV and UAT sign-off evidence.

p2-26.q: YAML pipelines define build and deployment as code in the repository (versioned, reviewed, branchable, reusable templates, multi-stage with environments and checks); classic release pipelines are configured in the web UI with a visual designer, which is easier to start with but harder to review, version and reuse. Microsoft's direction is YAML.
i: YAML templates (extends, stage templates) standardise pipelines across many services.
Environments with approvals, checks and deployment history replace classic stage approvals.
Classic still has features some teams rely on (gates UI, release variables per stage, easier artifact triggers), especially on older on-prem Azure DevOps Server.
Migration: export classic definitions and recreate as YAML stages step by step.
On our on-prem Azure DevOps Server we have [YAML builds and some classic release definitions], which the MCP server drives through the REST API.
f: Why does pipeline-as-code matter in GxP?
Pipeline changes are reviewed and versioned like application code, which supports change control.
What is an extends template?
A required base template that pipelines must extend, enforcing mandatory steps such as scans.

p2-27.q: We use short-lived feature branches from main merged through pull requests with build validation and reviews, release branches cut for each release (release/2024.3) where only fixes go, hotfix branches from the release tag, and annotated tags marking exactly what was released to each environment so builds are traceable.
i: Fixes on a release branch are merged back to main (or cherry-picked) so they are not lost.
Semantic versions in tags (v2024.3.1) and in artifacts.
Trunk-based development with feature flags is the alternative for faster delivery.
GitFlow's develop branch adds overhead; most teams simplified to main plus release branches.
As release integrator I merge team features, resolve conflicts and create the tags.
f: Why tag releases?
To reproduce exactly what is in production and to compare releases for audit and debugging.
Merge or rebase?
Squash or merge commits for PRs per team convention; never rewrite shared history.

p2-28.q: Ansible is an agentless automation tool that runs YAML playbooks over SSH or WinRM to configure servers and install software. In IRT our release installs ran through Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts across the multi-node environments; idempotency means running a task again leaves the same end state, so reruns after a failure are safe.
i: Modules are idempotent by design (copy, template, service: state=started); raw shell commands are not unless guarded with creates/removes or changed_when.
Inventories define nodes per environment; group_vars hold environment settings; Ansible Vault encrypts secrets.
Roles organise reusable steps; handlers restart services only when something changed.
--check and --diff do a dry run; serial controls rolling updates across nodes.
The MCP deployment tools trigger the same release stages that run these playbooks.
c:
- name: Deploy shipments service
  hosts: app_nodes
  serial: 1                      # one node at a time
  tasks:
    - name: Copy release package
      ansible.builtin.unarchive: { src: "shipments-{{ version }}.zip", dest: /opt/irt/shipments }
      notify: restart shipments
  handlers:
    - name: restart shipments
      ansible.builtin.service: { name: shipments, state: restarted }
f: Ansible vs Terraform?
Terraform provisions infrastructure; Ansible configures and deploys onto it.
How do you make a shell task idempotent?
Add creates: or a condition, or check state first and set changed_when properly.

p2-29.q: Rolling deployment replaces instances gradually with the new version; blue-green runs a full new environment (green) next to the old (blue) and switches traffic at once, allowing instant rollback; canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watches metrics, then increases gradually.
i: Rolling: cheap and default in ECS/Kubernetes; old and new versions run together briefly, so changes must be backward compatible.
Blue-green: double capacity during the switch; database must work for both versions.
Canary: needs good metrics and automated analysis (Argo Rollouts, CodeDeploy, App Mesh weights).
Feature flags complement all three by decoupling release from deployment.
IRT releases are rolling node by node in controlled windows, with verification after each node.
f: Which is safest for database changes?
Any, if you use expand/contract migrations so both versions work with the schema.
How do you roll back a canary?
Shift traffic back to the stable version automatically when error or latency thresholds break.

p2-30.q: I plan rollback so the application can roll back without rolling back the database: schema changes are backward compatible (expand/contract), applied before the app, and destructive steps happen only in a later release. If a database rollback is really needed, there is a tested down script or a restore point, decided in advance in the release plan.
i: Expand: add columns/tables (nullable or defaulted), deploy app writing both; contract: drop old structures in a later release.
Data migrations are reversible or backed up (copy tables) before running.
Practise rollback in UAT; document the decision criteria and owner.
Feature flags turn off new behaviour without a deployment.
In GxP the rollback plan is part of the change request and approved with it.
f: Why not just restore a backup?
You lose data written since the backup; it is the last resort.
How long do you keep the old columns?
At least one release after the app stops using them, so rollback remains possible.

p2-31.q: In GxP, every release follows change control: documented change requests with impact and risk assessment, traceability from requirements to tests, formal validation (FV) with evidence, independent QA and TechOps installs in qualified environments, UAT sign-off, approved deployment windows, and post-deployment verification, with everything recorded for audit.
i: Separation of duties: developers do not deploy to production themselves.
Only validated artifacts move forward; no rebuilds between environments.
Deviations and incidents are documented with CAPA (corrective and preventive actions).
Automation helps if it is itself controlled and validated (our MCP server keeps approvals in Azure DevOps).
Release cadence is slower and planned; hotfixes still need expedited change control.
f: What is CAPA?
Corrective and Preventive Action: fixing a problem and preventing recurrence, with documentation.
How do you speed things up in GxP?
Automate evidence collection, test early, and keep changes small and well-documented.

p2-32.q: Logs are timestamped records of discrete events with detail (errors, requests, business events); metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU) that are cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts; traces follow a single request across services as a tree of timed spans, showing where time and errors occur.
i: Use metrics to detect, traces to locate, logs to explain.
Correlate them: trace id in logs, exemplars in metrics linking to traces.
Cardinality: avoid high-cardinality labels (user id) in metrics; put those in logs and traces.
OpenTelemetry standardises all three signals.
f: Why not just logs?
Logs are expensive to query at scale and poor for trends; metrics alert faster and cheaper.
What are percentiles?
p95 latency means 95 percent of requests were faster; averages hide slow tails.

p2-33.q: CloudWatch is AWS's native monitoring: Logs (with Logs Insights queries), Metrics (AWS and custom), Alarms (with SNS actions), dashboards and X-Ray traces. Grafana is a visualisation layer that queries CloudWatch and other sources (Prometheus, Loki) in one place with richer dashboards and alerting. We use CloudWatch as the data store and Grafana for team dashboards.
i: Logs Insights: `fields @timestamp, @message | filter CorrelationId = "abc" | sort @timestamp`.
Metric filters turn log patterns into metrics (count of "SFTP transfer failed").
Embedded Metric Format lets apps emit metrics through structured logs.
Alarms: composite alarms reduce noise; anomaly detection for seasonal metrics.
Grafana: one dashboard per service with golden signals, plus business panels (shipments processed).
c:
fields @timestamp, level, message, CorrelationId
| filter service = "shipments-api" and level = "Error"
| stats count() by bin(5m)
f: How do you control CloudWatch Logs cost?
Retention policies, sensible log levels, and avoiding verbose debug logs in production.
Where do you look first in an incident?
The service's Grafana dashboard for golden signals, then Logs Insights for errors.

p2-34.q: The four golden signals from Google's SRE book are latency (how long requests take, separating successes and failures), traffic (demand, such as requests per second), errors (rate of failed requests) and saturation (how full the system is: CPU, memory, queue depth, connection pools). Monitoring them gives a quick health picture of any service.
i: RED method for services: Rate, Errors, Duration; USE method for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors.
Use percentiles (p95, p99) for latency, not averages.
Saturation predicts problems before errors appear (queue growth, pool exhaustion).
Business signals complete the picture (shipments processed per hour).
f: Which signal warns earliest?
Saturation, because queues and pools fill before latency and errors spike.
Why separate failed request latency?
Fast failures (instant 500s) can make average latency look better while things are broken.

p2-35.q: I start by stabilising (mitigate impact), then build a timeline, gather evidence (metrics, logs, traces, recent changes), form hypotheses and test them one at a time until I find a cause that explains every symptom; then I fix it, verify, and write a blameless post-mortem with actions so it does not recur.
i: Ask what changed: deployments, config, data volume, vendor behaviour, certificates.
5 whys or a fishbone diagram to go from symptom to root cause.
Reproduce in a lower environment when possible.
Distinguish trigger (the event) from root cause (the weakness) and contributing factors.
Example: the RabbitMQ outage: trigger = large vendor file and memory alarm; root cause = publishing without confirms; fix = publisher confirms plus alerts.
f: What is a blameless post-mortem?
A review focused on systems and processes, not individuals, so people share facts openly.
When is RCA complete?
When the cause explains all symptoms, the fix is verified and prevention actions are tracked.

p2-36.q: A good alert is actionable (someone must do something now), urgent, tied to user impact or an SLO, has a clear owner and a runbook link, fires rarely when nothing is wrong, and carries enough context (service, environment, dashboard link) to start immediately.
i: Alert on symptoms (error rate, latency SLO burn) rather than every cause (CPU 80 percent).
Use multi-window burn-rate alerts for SLOs to catch fast and slow burns.
Tune thresholds and durations to avoid flapping; review noisy alerts regularly.
Non-urgent issues go to tickets or dashboards, not pages.
Every alert should have a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate.
f: What is alert fatigue?
Too many low-value alerts make people ignore all alerts, including important ones.
Example of a good alert in IRT?
Shipment status messages in DLQ greater than zero for 10 minutes, linked to the replay runbook.

p2-37.q: Kafka is a distributed, append-only log: messages are retained for a period, consumers track their own offsets, many consumer groups can read the same stream and replay it, and ordering is per partition with very high throughput. RabbitMQ is a message broker with queues and flexible routing (exchanges), per-message acknowledgements, priorities and TTLs; messages are removed once consumed.
i: Kafka fits event streaming, multiple independent consumers, replay, audit-like history, analytics.
RabbitMQ fits task queues, commands, request/reply, complex routing, per-message retry and DLQ.
Scaling: Kafka by partitions; RabbitMQ by queues and competing consumers (quorum queues for HA).
RabbitMQ Streams add log-like replay; Kafka adds queue-like features in newer versions (share groups).
In IRT: Kafka for shipment status events consumed by several services; RabbitMQ for notifications and work queues.
f: Which gives ordering?
Kafka per partition (by key); RabbitMQ per queue with a single consumer.
Which is easier to operate?
RabbitMQ for small setups; Kafka is simpler as a managed service (MSK, Confluent).

p2-38.q: A topic is a named stream of events split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers and replicated. Producers choose the partition by key (same key, same partition, same order); a consumer group shares the partitions among its consumers so each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, while different groups read independently.
i: Parallelism is capped by partition count within a group.
Offsets are committed per group and partition; consumers resume from them after restarts.
Rebalancing reassigns partitions when consumers join or leave; cooperative rebalancing reduces pauses.
Choose keys for ordering needs (ShipmentId) and even distribution.
Retention by time or size, independent of consumption.
f: Can you reduce partitions?
No; you can only add them, and adding changes key-to-partition mapping for new messages.
What happens with two groups on one topic?
Each group gets every message, so different services can process the same events.

p2-39.q: RabbitMQ has four main exchange types: direct (routes to queues whose binding key equals the routing key), topic (pattern matching with * for one word and # for zero or more, like shipment.*.delivered), fanout (broadcasts to all bound queues, ignoring keys) and headers (routes on message header values). The default exchange routes directly to the queue named by the routing key.
i: Direct for commands to specific workers; topic for event categories; fanout for broadcast notifications.
Alternate exchanges catch unroutable messages; mandatory flag returns them to the publisher.
Dead-letter exchanges route rejected or expired messages.
Consistent-hash exchange (plugin) spreads by key for sharding.
c:
await channel.ExchangeDeclareAsync("shipments", ExchangeType.Topic, durable: true);
await channel.QueueBindAsync("notify-sites", "shipments", "shipment.*.delivered");
f: Which exchange for "every service gets every event"?
Fanout, or topic with # binding.
What happens to messages with no matching binding?
They are dropped, unless mandatory or an alternate exchange is used.

p2-40.q: Publisher confirms make RabbitMQ acknowledge each published message once it is safely stored (or nack it), so the publisher knows about failures instead of losing messages silently. In [mid-2024] a memory alarm blocked publishers and dropped connections, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates vanished without errors because we published without confirms; I recovered by replaying the vendor files (consumers upsert, so it was safe) and fixed it permanently with confirms, retries, alerts and memory tuning.
i: How confirms work: channel in confirm mode, each message gets a delivery tag, broker sends basic.ack or basic.nack; with persistent messages to durable or quorum queues the ack comes after writing to disk.
In RabbitMQ.Client 7, `CreateChannelOptions(publisherConfirmationsEnabled: true, publisherConfirmationTrackingEnabled: true)` makes BasicPublishAsync wait for the confirm and throw on nack.
Track asynchronously in batches to keep throughput; we saw about [5 percent] cost.
Full guarantee chain: durable queues, persistent messages, confirms, manual consumer acks, DLQ, idempotent consumers; plus an outbox for publish-after-commit.
Monitoring added: memory and disk alarms, blocked connections, publish vs deliver rates, and an alert when the incoming rate drops to zero during business hours.
f: What does the memory high watermark do?
When RabbitMQ memory exceeds it (default 40 percent of RAM, or a set value), the broker blocks publishing connections until memory drops.
Confirms vs transactions?
AMQP transactions also give safety but are much slower; confirms are the recommended approach.
w: I take ownership on support duty: restore service first, then fix the root cause.
I turn an incident into lasting guarantees and monitoring, not just a one-off fix.

p2-41.q: At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time (may be lost, never duplicated: ack before processing); at-least-once means it is never lost but may be duplicated (ack after processing, retry on failure); exactly-once means each message affects the system once, which in practice is achieved as effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
i: Most real systems choose at-least-once with idempotent consumers.
Kafka offers exactly-once semantics inside Kafka (idempotent producer plus transactions for read-process-write).
Across systems (Kafka to database) you need idempotency or storing offsets with the data in one transaction.
At-most-once fits metrics or telemetry where loss is acceptable.
f: Where can duplicates come from?
Producer retries, consumer crashes before committing, redelivery after timeouts.
How do you test idempotency?
Deliver the same message twice in an integration test and assert the state is unchanged.

p2-42.q: An idempotent consumer produces the same result if it processes the same message twice. I give every message a unique id and either record processed ids in a table (inbox pattern) in the same transaction as the business change, or design the change itself as an upsert or conditional update (set status where version is older) so repeats are harmless.
i: Inbox table: unique constraint on MessageId; insert fails for duplicates, so skip them.
Natural idempotency: "set shipment 881 to Delivered" is idempotent; "add 10 kits" is not, so carry the target state or a version.
Keep processed-id records for longer than the maximum redelivery window, then clean up.
External side effects (emails, API calls) need their own idempotency keys.
Our shipment consumers upsert status by shipment id, which is why replaying vendor files after the outage was safe.
c:
INSERT INTO dbo.InboxMessages (MessageId, ProcessedAt) VALUES (@MessageId, SYSUTCDATETIME()); -- unique key
UPDATE dbo.Shipments SET Status = @Status, StatusAt = @At
WHERE ShipmentId = @ShipmentId AND (StatusAt IS NULL OR StatusAt < @At);  -- ignore older/duplicate events
f: Why do this in one transaction?
So the business change and the processed marker succeed or fail together.
What about out-of-order messages?
Compare timestamps or versions and ignore stale updates, as in the WHERE clause.

p2-43.q: A dead-letter queue holds messages that could not be processed after retries (or that expired or were rejected), so they do not block the main queue or get lost. Operators inspect them, fix the cause and replay them; alerts fire when the DLQ is not empty.
i: RabbitMQ: queue argument x-dead-letter-exchange; messages rejected with requeue=false, expired by TTL or over a length limit go there; quorum queues add delivery limits.
SQS: redrive policy with maxReceiveCount and DLQ redrive back to the source.
Kafka: dead-letter topic written by the consumer code or the framework.
Store failure reason and attempt count in headers for diagnosis.
Poison messages (always failing) must go to the DLQ quickly instead of retrying forever.
f: What do you do with DLQ messages?
Investigate, fix code or data, then replay them with a tool or script, and document it.
Can retries cause DLQ storms?
Yes, if a dependency is down; use backoff and circuit breakers so transient outages do not dead-letter everything.

p2-44.q: The transactional outbox pattern saves the business change and the event to publish in the same database transaction (into an Outbox table); a separate relay then reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, marking them sent. This guarantees an event is published if and only if the change committed, without distributed transactions.
i: Delivery is at-least-once (the relay may publish twice after a crash), so consumers must be idempotent.
Relay options: polling background service, CDC (Debezium reading the transaction log), or libraries (MassTransit, NServiceBus, Wolverine outbox).
Keep ordering per aggregate by publishing in sequence per key.
Clean up old published rows.
Inbox pattern is the consumer-side mirror for deduplication.
f: Why not publish right after SaveChanges?
If publishing fails or the process crashes between the two, the event is lost while the data changed.
Polling vs CDC?
Polling is simple; CDC has lower latency and no polling load but needs more infrastructure.

p2-45.q: Authentication answers "who are you?" by verifying identity (password, SSO, token, certificate); authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" by checking permissions for that identity on a resource or action. In ASP.NET Core, UseAuthentication builds HttpContext.User and UseAuthorization enforces policies; failures return 401 and 403 respectively.
i: Role-based (RequireRole), claims-based and policy-based authorization; resource-based for "this user on this study".
Authorization must happen on the server for every request; UI hiding is not security.
Least privilege and separation of duties (e.g. unblinded vs blinded roles in clinical trials).
OAuth 2.0 is about delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication.
f: 401 Unauthorized actually means unauthenticated; 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not permitted.
Where do you check "user can access this study"?
In a resource-based authorization handler, using the study id from the request.

p2-46.q: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, signed token with three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm, key id), payload (claims such as sub, iss, aud, exp, roles) and signature. The API validates it by checking the signature with the issuer's public key (from JWKS), then issuer, audience, expiry and not-before, and only then trusts the claims.
i: Signed is not encrypted: anyone can read the payload, so never put secrets or PHI in it (JWE exists for encryption).
Reject alg "none" and enforce expected algorithms (RS256/ES256); never let the token choose a symmetric key.
Short lifetimes plus refresh tokens; revocation needs extra measures (our jti denylist).
Key rotation via kid and JWKS caching.
ASP.NET Core JwtBearer does all this; Part 10 shows the pipeline.
f: Access token vs ID token?
The access token is for APIs; the ID token tells the client app who logged in and must not be sent to APIs.
Where should a SPA store tokens?
In memory with a BFF or HttpOnly cookies, not localStorage.

p2-47.q: In the authorization code flow with PKCE, the app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code_challenge (a hash of a random code_verifier); the user logs in; the provider redirects back with a short-lived authorization code; the app exchanges the code plus the code_verifier at the token endpoint for tokens (ID token with OpenID Connect, access token, refresh token). PKCE proves the same app that started the flow is finishing it, so stolen codes are useless.
i: PKCE is recommended for all clients, including confidential ones (OAuth 2.1 makes it mandatory).
state parameter prevents CSRF; nonce protects the ID token from replay.
The implicit flow is deprecated; SPAs use code + PKCE or a backend-for-frontend.
Refresh token rotation detects token theft.
Machine-to-machine uses client credentials instead.
f: Why is the code exchanged on a back channel?
Tokens are not exposed in browser URLs or history.
What does the BFF pattern do?
A server-side component handles tokens and gives the SPA only a secure session cookie.

p2-48.q: JWTs stay valid until expiry even after logout because the API validates them statelessly. In [2024] a security review found tokens in one IRT module still worked [60 minutes] after logout; I cut access-token lifetime to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens server-side, added a jti denylist in ElastiCache with TTL equal to the remaining lifetime checked in OnTokenValidated, cleared cookies and ended the IdP session. Old tokens were rejected immediately, at about [1 ms] per request.
i: Denylist only stores logged-out tokens, so it stays tiny and keeps APIs mostly stateless.
Fail closed if Redis is unavailable (401 and re-login), with alerting.
Also revoke on password change, role removal or account disable.
Tests: unit test for the event handler, Playwright test replaying an old token after logout expecting 401.
Alternatives: reference tokens with introspection, or server-side sessions; heavier for many services.
f: Why not just shorten tokens to 1 minute?
Constant refreshes add load and complexity; short tokens plus a denylist is a better balance.
What is the end-session endpoint?
The OpenID Connect logout endpoint that ends the SSO session at the identity provider.
w: I balance security with performance and choose the smallest safe change.
I prove a security fix with automated tests, not just manual retest.

p2-49.q: Browsers send all cookies for a domain on every request, and servers cap total header size (IIS/http.sys around 16 KB in our setup); SSO auth cookies holding many role and group claims are chunked into several cookies and can exceed it, giving 400 "request header too long" for users in many groups. I fixed it by moving the auth ticket server-side with ITicketStore (cookie holds only a key), loading study permissions per request with cached claims transformation, and narrowing cookie domain and path, so the cookie dropped from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB].
i: Diagnosis: the pattern (only users with many studies) pointed to claim volume; a test user with many groups reproduced it.
Why not raise limits: the next user with more groups fails again, and every request carries kilobytes of cookie.
ITicketStore backed by [Redis/ElastiCache] with sliding expiry matching the session.
Claims transformation (IClaimsTransformation) adds permissions per request from a cache.
Result: tickets stopped, no user-visible change, released through the regulated process.
f: What is cookie chunking?
ASP.NET Core splits a large auth cookie into several cookies (.AspNetCore.CookiesC1, C2...) to stay under per-cookie size limits.
How did you verify the fix?
Test users with many groups in validation, header size measurements, and no new tickets after release.
w: I look for the pattern behind "random" user problems before changing configuration.
I prefer fixing the root cause over raising a limit.

p2-50.q: Reverse tabnabbing is when a page opened with target="_blank" uses window.opener to navigate the original tab, for example to a fake login page, while the user is looking at the new tab. The fix is rel="noopener noreferrer" on links and the noopener feature in window.open, plus Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy; modern browsers default to noopener for target="_blank", but explicit is safer.
i: noopener sets window.opener to null; noreferrer also hides the Referer header.
COOP: same-origin isolates your browsing context group from cross-origin popups.
ESLint react/jsx-no-target-blank prevents regressions in React code.
I fixed [about 40] links in IRT in [2024] and enabled the lint rule (full story in Part 6).
f: Why does it matter in a clinical app?
A phishing redirect of a logged-in study manager's tab could steal credentials.
Do modern browsers fix it?
Most default _blank links to noopener, but window.open and older browsers still need explicit protection.

p2-51.q: For APIs the most important risks (OWASP API Security Top 10 2023) are broken object level authorization (accessing another study's data by changing an id), broken authentication, broken object property level authorization (over-posting, excessive data exposure), unrestricted resource consumption, broken function level authorization, SSRF, security misconfiguration and unsafe consumption of third-party APIs. I prevent them with per-object authorization checks, DTOs, rate limits, validation and hardened configuration.
i: BOLA: every query filtered by what the caller may access (resource-based authorization), never trusting ids from the client.
Input validation and parameterised queries for injection.
Limits: payload size, page size, rate limits, timeouts.
Security headers, HTTPS only, no stack traces, least-privilege service accounts.
Inventory and version APIs so old endpoints do not stay exposed.
f: What is BOLA in practice?
GET /api/studies/42/subjects works for a user who has no access to study 42 because the API only checked login.
How do you test for it?
Automated tests calling endpoints as a user without access, expecting 403 or 404.

p2-52.q: XSS (cross-site scripting) injects malicious script into your pages so it runs in other users' browsers with their session; CSRF (cross-site request forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to your site, using their cookies. XSS abuses the user's trust in the site; CSRF abuses the site's trust in the user's browser.
i: XSS defences: output encoding (React does it), sanitising HTML (DOMPurify), CSP, HttpOnly cookies.
CSRF defences: SameSite cookies (Lax default in modern browsers), anti-forgery tokens for cookie-authenticated forms, checking Origin headers.
Bearer tokens in Authorization headers are not sent automatically, so token APIs are not CSRF-prone, but tokens in JS are XSS-prone.
ASP.NET Core: [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] and AddAntiforgery for cookie-auth endpoints.
f: Can XSS bypass CSRF protection?
Yes; script running on your origin can read tokens and send requests.
What does SameSite=Lax allow?
Cookies on top-level GET navigations from other sites, but not on cross-site POSTs or iframes.

p2-53.q: Secrets live in a managed store (AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store SecureString, Azure Key Vault, Azure DevOps secret variables), are loaded at runtime by the service's IAM role, never committed to Git or baked into images, rotated regularly, scoped per environment with least-privilege access, masked in logs, and audited.
i: Local development: user secrets or a local .env excluded from Git.
Rotation: Secrets Manager rotates RDS credentials automatically; apps re-read on failure.
Detection: secret scanning in CI (GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks) and pre-commit hooks.
Avoid environment variables for very sensitive values where possible (visible in process listings and task definitions); fetch at runtime.
In the MCP server each user's PAT comes from their environment, never from files in the repo.
f: What if a secret is committed?
Rotate it immediately, then remove it from history; assume it is compromised.
Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store?
Secrets Manager adds rotation and cross-account sharing at a cost; Parameter Store is cheaper for config and simple secrets.

p2-54.q: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard (introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, now widely adopted) that lets AI applications connect to external tools and data in a uniform way. An MCP server exposes tools (actions), resources (readable data) and prompts over JSON-RPC 2.0; any MCP host such as Cursor, Claude, VS Code Copilot or ChatGPT can discover and call them, so one integration works with many AI clients.
i: Transports: stdio for local servers launched by the host, and Streamable HTTP for remote servers (it replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport).
Lifecycle: initialize handshake with capability negotiation, then tools/list and tools/call.
Tools have a name, description and JSON Schema input; results are content blocks, optionally structured output.
Remote servers use OAuth 2.1 based authorization in the spec.
Official SDKs exist for C#/.NET (ModelContextProtocol package), TypeScript, Python and more.
Analogy: "USB-C for AI tools": the host is the laptop, servers are peripherals.
f: MCP vs function calling?
Function calling is a model feature inside one app; MCP standardises how tools are packaged and discovered across apps.
Tools vs resources?
Tools perform actions with side effects; resources are data the host can read into context.

p2-55.q: The CIRT MCP server lets AI agents run build, release and multi-node deployment operations on our on-prem Azure DevOps Server. About 77 tools are grouped by domain (builds, releases, approvals, multi-node deployments, artifacts, environment checks, logs), each with a precise name, description and typed schema, wrapping the Azure DevOps REST APIs with the caller's own permissions; it cut deployment time from 6 hours to 2 and people per deployment from 6 to 1.
i: Naming convention verb_noun by domain (queue_build, get_release_status, deploy_release_stage) so the model picks correctly.
Descriptions say when to use the tool and what it returns; parameters have enums and examples [for environments FV, TechOps, UAT, Prod].
Outputs are short structured summaries (status, failing step, link), not raw JSON dumps, to save context.
Long operations return an id and a status tool to poll, avoiding timeouts.
Composite tools [for "deploy to environment and verify versions on all nodes"] reduce many-step mistakes.
Built in [C# with the official MCP SDK over stdio], packaged so teammates install with one command.
f: Why so many tools instead of a few generic ones?
Specific tools with tight schemas are easier for the model to use correctly and easier to secure than one "run any API call" tool.
How did you test it?
Unit tests for each tool's validation and mapping, plus dry runs against non-production environments before UAT.
w: I spot a manual, error-prone process and automate it end to end.
I design tools for both the AI and the humans who must trust it.

p2-56.q: I make it safe through least privilege (each user's own Azure DevOps credentials, no shared admin token), separating read-only from write tools, requiring explicit confirmation and keeping human approval gates for production, validating every input against schemas and allow-lists, adding timeouts and idempotency, logging every tool call, and never returning secrets.
i: Prompt injection risk: logs or work items can contain text that tries to instruct the agent, so tools treat outputs as data and sensitive actions always need confirmation.
Allow-lists for environments, pipelines and nodes; reject anything else.
Dry-run modes show what would happen first.
Rate limits and concurrency limits avoid accidental floods (one deployment per environment at a time).
Audit log: who, which tool, which parameters, result, timestamp; supports GxP traceability.
MCP hosts also ask the user to approve tool calls; we do not rely on that alone.
f: What is the confused deputy problem here?
A server with broad rights doing things on behalf of a user who should not have them; using the caller's own token avoids it.
Could the agent deploy to production by mistake?
No; production stages still require Azure DevOps approvals by authorised people.

p2-57.q: A good tool definition has a clear, unique, action-oriented name; a description saying what it does, when to use it (and when not), and what it returns; a small, strongly typed input schema with enums, defaults and examples; concise, structured output with actionable error messages; and predictable, safe behaviour (idempotent where possible).
i: Fewer, well-scoped tools beat many overlapping ones; overlapping tools confuse models.
Errors should tell the agent what to do next ("Release 123 is waiting for approval by QA").
Keep outputs small: summaries and ids, with separate tools for details.
Annotations like readOnlyHint and destructiveHint in MCP help hosts decide on confirmation.
Test with real prompts and watch which tool the model chooses.
f: What is the most common mistake?
Vague descriptions and huge raw outputs that waste context and lead to wrong tool choices.
How do you version tools?
Add new tools or optional parameters rather than changing behaviour of existing ones.

p2-58.q: I use Copilot inline completions for boilerplate, mappings and tests, and Cursor chat and agent mode for explaining unfamiliar code, multi-file refactors, upgrade chores and drafting SQL, YAML and scripts, guided by project rules for our conventions. I always review, build and test the output, because I own every line I commit.
i: Cursor rules files hold our coding standards and architecture notes so suggestions match the codebase.
MCP servers (including ours) let the agent check builds and deployments from the editor.
Good uses: test generation, regex and LINQ drafts, log summarisation, migration scaffolding, PR descriptions.
Avoid pasting secrets or patient data; use company-approved tools and settings.
Example: the [.NET 10 upgrade] used agent mode for repetitive package and API changes, reviewed file by file.
f: Has AI ever produced wrong code for you?
Yes, for example plausible but non-existent APIs or missing null checks; tests and review caught them.
Does it make you less skilled?
No, I use it for speed on known work and still reason through design and correctness myself.

p2-59.q: I treat AI code like code from a new teammate: read every line, check it compiles and passes tests (and write tests for edge cases), verify APIs and packages exist and are current, run static analysis and security scans (SonarQube, dependency checks), and look for the common AI mistakes: injection, missing authorization, hardcoded secrets, swallowed exceptions and outdated patterns.
i: Hallucinated packages are a supply-chain risk ("slopsquatting"); confirm every new dependency.
Check licences of suggested code and packages.
Compare with official documentation for version-specific behaviour (.NET 8 vs 10).
Same pull request review and quality gates as all code; no special path for AI code.
f: How do you check accuracy for business logic?
Against requirements and with tests built from real scenarios, not just the AI's own tests.
Who is responsible for AI-written bugs?
The developer who committed it.

p2-60.q: I give clear context and a specific goal, constraints and the expected output format; provide examples (few-shot); break big tasks into steps and ask for a plan first; give the model the relevant code, docs or errors; ask it to state assumptions and to verify its own output; and iterate based on results.
i: Role and audience: "You are reviewing a .NET 10 API for security issues".
Structured outputs (JSON schema) for anything parsed by code.
Ground answers in provided documents; ask it to say "unknown" when unsure.
Project rule files and reusable prompt templates for the team (the MCP README has [10] example prompts).
For agents: clear stopping criteria and limits.
f: Chain-of-thought?
Asking the model to reason step by step improves complex answers; modern reasoning models do this internally.
Zero-shot vs few-shot?
Zero-shot gives only instructions; few-shot adds examples of input and desired output.

p2-61.q: RAG retrieves relevant pieces of your own documents at question time and gives them to the LLM as context, so answers are grounded in current, private data without retraining. The pipeline: split documents into chunks, create embeddings, store them in a vector index; at query time embed the question, retrieve the most similar chunks (often hybrid with keyword search and re-ranking), and prompt the model to answer from them with citations.
i: Chunking size and overlap strongly affect quality.
Hybrid search (BM25 plus vectors) and a re-ranker improve relevance.
Access control must apply at retrieval so users only see documents they may see.
Evaluate with test questions: retrieval recall, answer faithfulness, citations.
Vector stores: Azure AI Search, OpenSearch, pgvector, Qdrant.
Example idea: [a RAG assistant over IRT SOPs and release runbooks].
f: RAG vs fine-tuning?
RAG adds knowledge that changes; fine-tuning changes behaviour or style; they can be combined.
Why do RAG systems still hallucinate?
Poor retrieval or the model ignoring context; fix retrieval and instruct it to answer only from sources.

p2-62.q: An agent is an LLM running in a loop: it plans, calls tools, observes the results and repeats until the goal is met. Agentic orchestration coordinates one or more agents (planner, executor, reviewer) with their tools, memory, step limits and permissions. AutoGen (Microsoft) provides multi-agent conversation patterns; Claude Code is a terminal coding agent that can use MCP servers; I apply these to engineering workflows such as deployments and code tasks.
i: Patterns: single agent with tools, planner-executor, supervisor with specialists, reviewer loops.
Guardrails: step and cost limits, allow-listed tools, human-in-the-loop for risky actions.
Observability: log every step and tool call for debugging and audit.
Microsoft Agent Framework (2025) brings together AutoGen and Semantic Kernel concepts for .NET and Python.
Our deployment agent flow: [plan the release, queue builds, deploy stage by stage, verify versions, report].
f: When not to use agents?
When a fixed script works reliably; agents add value when steps vary or need judgement.
Biggest risk?
Loops and unintended actions, controlled with limits, confirmations and least privilege.

p2-63.q: Azure OpenAI (now part of Azure AI Foundry) runs OpenAI models inside the company's Azure tenant with enterprise controls: Entra ID auth, private endpoints, regional data residency, content filtering, and data not used for training. Direct provider APIs may get new models first and are simpler for prototypes. For a regulated healthcare company the enterprise controls usually decide.
i: Compare: model availability and versions, quotas and rate limits, pricing (provisioned throughput vs pay-as-you-go), compliance certifications, network isolation.
Abstraction layers (Microsoft.Extensions.AI IChatClient) make it easy to switch providers in .NET.
Monitor cost, latency and token usage either way.
Patient data rules (HIPAA, GDPR) and company policy decide what can be sent.
f: What is provisioned throughput?
Reserved model capacity with predictable latency, billed per unit instead of per token.
Can you use Claude in Azure?
Azure AI Foundry hosts many models; AWS Bedrock offers Claude and others in AWS.

p2-64.q: I ground the model in trusted data (RAG, tool calls for facts), give clear instructions with permission to say "I don't know", use structured outputs validated by code, keep temperature low for factual tasks, check outputs with rules or a second pass, show sources, keep humans approving important actions, and measure quality with evaluation sets over time.
i: Tools for anything factual or current: let the model call an API rather than remember.
Validate: JSON schema, business rules, allow-lists before acting.
Evals: golden question sets, regression checks when prompts or models change.
Narrow tasks are more reliable than open-ended ones.
Monitor production: feedback buttons, logs of prompts and outputs (without sensitive data).
f: Can hallucinations be eliminated?
No, only reduced and contained by validation and human review.
Example in your MCP server?
Build and release status always come from tool calls to Azure DevOps, never from the model's guess.

p2-65.q: Teammates kept the manual, multi-person process out of habit and caution, so I made adoption easy and safe instead of mandatory: a [30-minute] live demo on a real UAT deployment, a README with [10] example prompts, pairing with the first [4] engineers, a chat thread for questions, and adding the tools people asked for. Within [about two months] most release deployments used it: 6 hours to 2, 6 people to 1.
i: Addressed fear directly: own permissions, confirmations before risky steps, existing approvals unchanged, everything logged.
Started with low-risk environments (FV, TechOps) before UAT and production.
Measured results to show value (time and people per deployment).
Feedback loop: the "fetch logs for a failed step" tool came from a teammate's request.
Champions: the first users helped others.
f: What would you do differently?
Involve QA and TechOps earlier so their concerns shaped the design from day one.
How do you measure adoption?
Share of release deployments run through the tool and time per deployment.
w: I lead change by example and by removing friction, not by authority.
I take people's concerns seriously and design safety in.

p2-66.q: A monolith is one deployable unit: simple to build, test, deploy and debug, with in-process calls and one database. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services around business capabilities, each owning its data, enabling independent scaling and team autonomy at the cost of distributed-system complexity (network failures, eventual consistency, observability, many pipelines).
i: A modular monolith (clear modules, enforced boundaries) is often the best start.
Split when teams block each other, parts need different scaling or release cadence.
Microservices need automation, monitoring, tracing and contracts before they pay off.
Avoid the distributed monolith: services that must deploy together or share a database.
IRT has [about a dozen] services such as randomization, supply and shipments, notifications.
f: What is Conway's law?
Systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them.
How do you split a monolith?
Strangler fig: route one capability at a time to a new service.

p2-67.q: The core is POST /studies/{studyId}/subjects/{subjectId}/randomize with an idempotency key, allowed only for authorised site users. In one database transaction it loads the study's randomization scheme (blocked or stratified lists), allocates the next free slot with locking so two sites never get the same slot, assigns a drug kit from site inventory, writes an immutable audit record and stores a SubjectRandomized event in the outbox. Non-functionals: blinding, high availability, validation and full audit.
i: Concurrency: SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) on the next slot, or a unique constraint on (StudyId, SlotNumber) with retry.
Stratification: separate lists per stratum (site, age group); dynamic methods like minimisation need careful algorithms.
Blinding: treatment arm hidden from most roles; only unblinded roles or emergency unblinding with reason and audit.
Idempotency key stored with the result so retries return the same allocation.
Downstream via outbox: resupply checks, notifications, EDC integration.
Availability: multi-AZ database, no single points of failure; randomization is the most critical path.
c:
SELECT TOP (1) SlotId, Arm FROM dbo.RandomizationSlots WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK, READPAST)
WHERE ListId = @ListId AND SubjectId IS NULL ORDER BY SlotNumber;
f: Why READPAST?
Concurrent requests skip slots locked by others instead of waiting, while order is preserved per list.
What if no kit is available at the site?
Fail the randomization cleanly or follow the study's rule, and trigger urgent resupply alerts.

p2-68.q: I model shipments from depots to sites with kits, quantities and statuses (Requested, Shipped, In Transit, Delivered, Received, Quarantined); resupply rules (trigger and resupply levels per site, forecast from enrolment) create shipment requests; vendor and courier status updates arrive via SFTP files and APIs, are processed idempotently through events, and the site confirms receipt with temperature data; dashboards and alerts flag delays and low stock.
i: State machine with allowed transitions; reject invalid ones.
Integration: [SFTP poller every 5 minutes] for depot files, Kafka events for status updates to several services.
Expiry dating and temperature excursions: quarantine kits pending review.
Indexes for site and study shipment lists (the [9 s to under 300 ms] fix).
Audit every status change with source (vendor file, user).
f: How do you handle duplicate vendor status files?
File hash dedup and idempotent upserts by shipment id and timestamp.
What triggers resupply?
Site inventory dropping below the trigger level, considering kits in transit and expected enrolment.

p2-69.q: The client uploads the file to S3 with a presigned URL (or to the API for small files), the API creates an import job and returns 202 with a job id; a worker streams and parses rows (CsvHelper), validates schema and business rules collecting per-row errors, then writes valid data in batches inside a transaction (we chose all-or-nothing with the business), reports status and an error file, audits who imported what, and uses a file hash for idempotency.
i: Streaming parse keeps memory flat even for large files; our typical file is [5 MB, ~10,000 rows].
Bulk insert with SqlBulkCopy into a staging table, then validate and merge set-based.
Concurrency limit [2 per user] and a global worker limit protect the database.
Progress endpoint or SignalR for status; error report as CSV with row numbers.
Security: size limits, content checks, CSV injection protection in exported files (prefix =, +, -, @).
f: All-or-nothing vs partial?
All-or-nothing keeps clinical data consistent; partial suits independent rows, with clear reporting.
How do you scale to very large files?
Split into chunks processed in parallel into staging, then one final merge.

p2-70.q: The API gateway pattern puts one entry point in front of many services to handle routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS and cross-cutting policies. Backend-for-frontend (BFF) gives each client type (web SPA, mobile, partner) its own tailored gateway that aggregates calls and shapes responses for that client, and for SPAs keeps tokens on the server.
i: Tools: AWS API Gateway, YARP (.NET reverse proxy), Azure API Management, Kong, Envoy.
Gateway should stay thin: no business logic, or it becomes a bottleneck.
BFF reduces chatty calls and over-fetching from mobile clients.
BFF security pattern: SPA uses an HttpOnly cookie session; BFF holds OAuth tokens and calls APIs.
c:
builder.Services.AddReverseProxy().LoadFromConfig(builder.Configuration.GetSection("ReverseProxy"));
app.MapReverseProxy();   // YARP routes /api/shipments/** to the shipments cluster
f: Gateway vs service mesh?
Gateway handles north-south (client to service) traffic; mesh handles east-west traffic between services.
One BFF per team or per client?
Per client experience, usually owned by the team building that client.

p2-71.q: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed data store must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error response); partition tolerance is unavoidable in real networks. So the real choice is CP or AP behaviour when partitions happen.
i: PACELC extends it: Else (no partition) you trade Latency vs Consistency.
CP examples: traditional relational with synchronous replication, ZooKeeper, etcd; AP examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB default eventually consistent reads.
Many systems are tunable (DynamoDB strongly consistent reads, Cassandra quorum).
In IRT, randomization and kit assignment need consistency (CP behaviour); dashboards and notifications tolerate eventual consistency.
f: Is CAP about all consistency models?
It uses linearizability; weaker models allow different trade-offs.
Why is "CA" not realistic?
Networks do partition, so a distributed system must decide what to do when they do.

p2-72.q: A saga manages a business transaction across several services as a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or message that triggers the next; if a step fails, compensating actions undo the earlier steps. It replaces distributed transactions (2PC) in microservices. Sagas are either choreographed (services react to events) or orchestrated (a central coordinator tells each service what to do).
i: Choreography: simple for few steps, but flow is hard to see; orchestration: explicit state, easier to monitor.
Compensations are semantic undos (cancel shipment), not database rollbacks, and must be idempotent.
Use outbox for reliable messaging and correlation ids per saga.
Tools: MassTransit state machines, NServiceBus sagas, AWS Step Functions, Temporal.
Example: [randomize subject, reserve kit, create shipment request, notify site]; if kit reservation fails, mark randomization pending and alert.
f: Saga vs 2PC?
2PC locks resources across systems and is fragile; sagas accept eventual consistency with compensation.
What about isolation?
Sagas lack it; use semantic locks (status Pending) and design for intermediate states.

p2-73.q: Every create, update and delete records who, what (old and new values), when (synchronised UTC time), where (source system, IP) and why (reason for change when required), in an append-only, tamper-evident store that users cannot edit or delete, captured automatically (EF Core SaveChanges interceptor, temporal tables or triggers) plus business events, searchable for inspections and retained as regulation requires (21 CFR Part 11, EU Annex 11).
i: Electronic signatures: re-authentication, meaning of signature, linked to the record.
Tamper evidence: hash chaining of records, WORM storage (S3 Object Lock) for archives, restricted database permissions.
Include correlation id so audit entries link to logs and traces.
Audit failures should block the change (same transaction), not silently skip.
SQL Server temporal tables give automatic history for row versions; combine with user context.
f: Audit log vs application log?
Audit logs are regulated business records with retention and integrity rules; application logs are for operations.
How do you show it is tamper-evident?
Hash chain verification and restricted permissions shown in validation evidence.

p2-74.q: I decide the key (user, client, IP, tenant), the limit and algorithm (token bucket for bursts, sliding window for smoothness, concurrency limit for expensive work), where to enforce (gateway for coarse limits, service for business limits), and shared state for multiple instances (Redis with atomic scripts). Rejected requests get 429 with Retry-After, and limits are monitored and tuned.
i: Algorithms: fixed window (simple, bursty at edges), sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket.
Distributed: Redis INCR with expiry or Lua scripts; or accept per-instance approximate limits.
ASP.NET Core built-in limiter is per instance (Part 10 shows code).
Different tiers for different clients; exempt health checks and internal calls.
Example: [concurrency limit 2 per user on CSV import].
f: Fail open or closed if Redis is down?
Usually fail open for availability, with alerts, unless the limit protects something critical.
Why Retry-After?
Well-behaved clients back off correctly instead of hammering.

p2-75.q: AI hosts (Cursor, Claude, Copilot) talk MCP to the CIRT MCP server [over stdio]; the server wraps Azure DevOps Server REST APIs for builds, releases, approvals and environments plus node-level deployment steps; an orchestration layer runs a deployment plan per environment across nodes, polls status, retries safe steps and stops on failure with a clear report; cross-cutting concerns are the user's own credentials, human approvals before production, a log of every action and structured outputs for the agent.
i: Requirements: cut [6-hour, 6-person] deployments, keep GxP approvals, work on on-prem Azure DevOps Server.
Components: tool layer (about 77 tools), Azure DevOps client with retries and timeouts, deployment plan model, status poller, audit logger.
Long-running work: start returns an id; status tool polls; no tool blocks for hours.
Failure handling: idempotent steps, resume from the failed step, clear human-readable reports.
Scaling: each user runs their own instance; Azure DevOps remains the source of truth and does the actual work.
Result: 6 hours to 2, 6 people to 1.
f: Why not a web portal instead?
Engineers already work in AI-enabled editors; MCP let them describe intent in plain language while reusing existing pipelines.
What would you add next?
A remote HTTP deployment with central audit and SSO, and richer pre-deployment checks.

p2-76.q: High availability means removing single points of failure and recovering automatically: multiple instances across availability zones behind load balancers with health checks, Multi-AZ databases with automatic failover, stateless services, retries with backoff and circuit breakers, queues to absorb spikes, graceful degradation, and tested backups and disaster recovery with defined RTO and RPO.
i: Availability targets: 99.9 percent is about 8.8 hours downtime a year; 99.99 percent about 53 minutes.
Redundancy at every layer: DNS, load balancer, compute, data, messaging (quorum queues, Kafka replication).
Deployments without downtime: rolling or blue-green with readiness checks.
Bulkheads isolate failures; timeouts everywhere.
Test it: failover drills, chaos experiments, game days.
f: RTO vs RPO?
RTO is how long you can be down; RPO is how much data (time) you can lose.
Multi-AZ vs multi-region?
Multi-AZ covers data-centre failures; multi-region covers regional outages at much higher cost and complexity.

p3-1.q: I'm a backend-focused full-stack engineer with about 5.5 years of experience, the last 4+ at IQVIA building C#/.NET microservices and APIs for IRT, a regulated clinical-trial platform for randomization, drug supply and shipments, on AWS with Docker and Azure DevOps CI/CD. My highlight is the CIRT MCP server I designed and built alone: about 77 tools that let AI agents run our builds and multi-node deployments, cutting deployments from 6 hours to 2 and from 6 people to 1. I'm now looking for a senior backend role where I own design and delivery.
i: Structure: present (role and domain), proof (one or two numbers), past (DXC start), future (why this role); keep it under 2 minutes.
Pick three proof points to plant hooks for follow-ups: MCP server (6h to 2h), RabbitMQ outage RCA, CSV bulk import live in production.
Mention the regulated (GxP) angle: it signals quality, testing discipline and audit awareness.
Tailor the last line to the job description (cloud, APIs, AI tooling, scale).
Avoid reading the resume line by line or personal life history.
f: What are you most proud of?
The MCP server: I spotted the problem, built it alone and got the team to adopt it, with measurable results.
Why backend-focused if you also do front end?
My depth is in APIs, data and distributed systems; I do front-end work to own features end to end.
w: I can summarise complex work clearly and lead with impact.
I know what I want next and why I am ready for it.

p3-2.q: I finished my B.Tech in Computer Science in 2020, joined DXC Technology in March 2021 building C#/.NET Framework solutions on SharePoint with production support, and moved to IQVIA in July 2022 as Software Development Engineer 2, where I build .NET Core microservices, Node and Python services, React and Angular UI on AWS, own release integration, do production RCA and built the MCP deployment server. Each move added scope: features, then services, then releases and platform tooling.
i: Tell it as a story of growing ownership, not a list of employers.
One concrete highlight per stage: DXC (SharePoint workflow automation, ITIL support), IQVIA (CSV import, RabbitMQ RCA, MCP server, .NET 10 upgrade [early 2026]).
Be ready to explain the gap between graduation (2020) and DXC (March 2021) honestly and briefly [e.g. job search, certifications and personal projects during the pandemic hiring freeze].
Finish with the bridge to this role.
f: Which role taught you the most?
IQVIA: distributed systems, cloud and regulated release discipline.
What did DXC give you that still helps?
Production support discipline and working within client processes.
w: I grow steadily in scope and responsibility.

p3-3.q: When a new medicine is tested, patients at hospitals worldwide are randomly assigned to receive it or a comparison treatment. IRT is the system that makes that assignment fairly and secretly, tells the hospital which numbered drug kit to give, and makes sure every hospital always has enough stock by triggering shipments from depots, while tracking those shipments. Because it affects patient safety and trial results, every change is validated and every action is audited.
i: Analogy: a fair lottery plus an automatic stock manager for a global pharmacy chain, where nobody knows who got what.
Blinding: doctors and patients don't know the treatment; kit numbers hide it.
Interactive Response Technology used to mean phone systems (IVRS); now it's web-based.
Regulation: GxP, 21 CFR Part 11 (electronic records and signatures), audit trails.
Shows you understand the business, not just the code.
f: What happens if IRT is down?
Sites can't randomize or dispense, which can delay patient treatment, so availability and support matter.
What is eConsent?
Electronic informed consent: patients review and sign trial consent digitally with an audit trail.
w: I can explain technical work to non-technical people.

p3-4.q: I'm a Software Development Engineer 2 in a roughly 100-member engineering organisation. I design and build .NET services and APIs, fix production issues, own release integration and verification (merging, tagging and running automated multi-node installs through FV, TechOps, UAT and production), built and own the CIRT MCP deployment server, and review code, mentor developers and take part in PI planning, grooming and demos.
i: Use "I" for your own work and "we" for team outcomes; interviewers listen for your part.
Typical week: [feature work on a service, a couple of PR reviews a day, a release verification, refinement and a demo].
Ownership areas: SFTP integration component, CSV bulk import, study-transfer guard, security fixes, MCP server.
Mentoring: onboarded [two graduate developers in 2024].
f: Who do you report to?
[An engineering manager, with a tech lead for day-to-day technical direction].
How big is your scrum team?
[About 8 people: developers, QA and a BA] within the ~100-member organisation.
w: I own outcomes across development, release and production, not just tickets.

p3-5.q: At DXC I learned enterprise .NET and client processes, but the work was mostly SharePoint customisation and support. I wanted to build modern cloud-based microservices on a product used globally, and IQVIA IRT gave me .NET Core, AWS, messaging and a regulated domain where quality really matters.
i: Keep it positive: moving towards growth, never complaining about the old employer.
Connect the move to what you then achieved (services, releases, MCP server).
Shows a pattern of deliberate career choices.
f: Would you go back to SharePoint work?
I value what I learned, but my focus now is backend services and cloud.
What did you learn in the switch?
Moving from .NET Framework to .NET Core, containers and AWS quickly by building real features.
w: I make deliberate choices to grow my skills.

p3-6.q: SDE 2 is IQVIA's internal level; my headline describes the scope I actually work at: designing services, solely building the MCP platform, owning release integration across application, APIs, database and UI, mentoring, and leading production RCAs. I'm targeting a senior role because I already do much of that work.
i: Let evidence carry it: specific ownership examples, not titles.
Different companies map levels differently; IQVIA's SDE 2 [covers 3 to 6 years of experience].
Never claim a title you didn't hold on official records; explain scope instead.
Turn it into a strength: "I'm ready for the title because I already do the job".
f: What senior behaviours do you show today?
Designing solutions, mentoring, owning incidents and releases, and driving adoption across the team.
What would you need to grow into staff level?
Broader cross-team architecture ownership and influence across several teams.
w: I'm honest about titles and confident about scope.

p3-7.q: Users reach the IRT web UI (Angular modules and React components) and vendors connect through integrations; traffic enters through API Gateway and load balancers with SSO-based authentication; .NET Core microservices for randomization, supply and shipments (plus Node and Python services and some legacy WCF) run on ECS; data lives in SQL Server/RDS and DynamoDB, events flow through Kafka and RabbitMQ, vendor files arrive over SFTP, and CloudWatch and Grafana provide monitoring.
i: Draw it left to right: clients, edge, services, data and messaging, integrations, observability.
Mention cross-cutting concerns: correlation ids, audit trail, secrets in Secrets Manager, CI/CD via Azure DevOps.
Pick one flow to walk through end to end: randomize subject, assign kit, publish event, notify site.
Describe only what you can defend in detail; say "I worked mainly on X" for areas you know less.
Show trade-offs: Kafka for shipment events with several consumers, RabbitMQ for work queues.
f: Where are the bottlenecks?
Database-heavy reporting queries and vendor file bursts; we addressed them with indexes, queues and scaling.
How do services communicate?
REST for queries and commands that need an answer, events for state changes.
w: I understand the whole system, not just my own service.

p3-8.q: Deployments on our on-prem Azure DevOps Server were manual and multi-node, took about 6 hours and needed about 6 people. I built the CIRT MCP server: about 77 typed tools for builds, releases and multi-node deployments, wrapping Azure DevOps APIs and our install scripts, with status polling, structured outputs and human approval for risky steps, packaged as a .NET tool. Deployment time fell from 6 hours to 2 and people per deployment from 6 to 1.
i: Why MCP: one server works across Cursor, Claude Code and Copilot; engineers describe intent in plain language.
How: C# MCP SDK, stdio transport, tools grouped by domain, long operations return ids plus status tools.
Safety: each user's own PAT, read vs write tools, confirmations, approvals unchanged, audit log of every call.
Adoption: demo, README with [10] prompts, pairing, feature requests turned into tools.
Measured on [8 vs 8] comparable deployments from release history.
f: What would you do differently?
Involve QA and TechOps earlier and add a central audit store from day one.
Is it still in use?
Yes, most of our team's release deployments run through it.
w: I find high-leverage problems and solve them end to end.
I measure impact instead of claiming it.

p3-9.q: My lead wanted evidence, so I compared [8] deployments from the [two release cycles] before the tool with [8] similar deployments from the [next two cycles] using it, on the same environments and node counts, using Azure DevOps release start and end timestamps and deployment-call attendee lists. Average time fell from about 6 hours to about 2, and people from 6 to 1; approvals and validation still need humans.
i: Like-for-like comparison: same environments and [4 to 6] nodes, similar release size.
Data source was the system of record, not memory or estimates.
Be honest about limits: small sample, some improvement from better scripts too.
Business translation: [about 20 person-hours to 2 per deployment].
f: Could other factors explain the gain?
Some, like script fixes, but the person count dropped because the agent runs the steps one person used to coordinate.
How would you measure it better now?
Log every deployment's start, end and operator automatically through the tool.
w: I back claims with data and state limitations honestly.

p3-10.q: The hardest part was designing tool boundaries so the model reliably chose the right one among about 77: naming, descriptions and schemas mattered more than code. Next were long-running deployments (start returns an id, status tools poll), differences and authentication quirks of on-prem Azure DevOps Server APIs, and keeping humans in control of production steps.
i: Fix for wrong tool choices: verb_noun naming, "use when" in descriptions, enums for environments, removing overlapping tools.
Context budget: summarised outputs instead of raw JSON logs.
On-prem API versions differ from Azure DevOps Services docs; I tested each call against our server.
Safety design: read-only tools first, write tools with confirmation, production via existing approvals.
f: How did you test tool selection?
Ran real prompts from teammates and logged which tools the agent called, then adjusted descriptions.
What failed in early versions?
The agent sometimes polled too aggressively; I added recommended wait times in tool outputs.
w: I solve ambiguous design problems by iterating with real users.

p3-11.q: The first version ran from my clone and teammates' copies drifted, so I packaged the CIRT MCP server as a .NET global tool published to our internal Azure Artifacts feed by its own pipeline on every tag. Teammates run dotnet tool install -g and add one entry to their Cursor or Claude Code MCP config; the server URL and each person's PAT come from environment variables. Setup went from [about an hour] to [about 10 minutes], with everyone on the same version.
i: PackAsTool and ToolCommandName in the csproj; semantic versions and release notes.
dotnet tool update -g for upgrades; health_check tool confirms connectivity and permissions.
No secrets in config files or the repo.
f: Why not a Docker image?
A global tool is simpler for developers' machines and starts instantly over stdio.
How do you ship a breaking change?
New major version with release notes, and keep old tool names working for a release.
w: I think about the user experience of internal tools, not just features.

p3-12.q: IRT exchanges data files with external vendors over SFTP. I owned a component that supports three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, behind one ISftpClient abstraction (connect, upload, download, list, delete); a factory picks the provider from per-vendor configuration so callers never change, and a base class holds shared retry, logging and error mapping. I released the Rebex provider to production.
i: Patterns: strategy + factory + template method; adapter per library.
Error mapping turns library-specific exceptions into our own (AuthFailed, HostKeyMismatch, Timeout).
Host key pinning per vendor; keys and passwords from Secrets Manager.
Atomic upload: write to a temp name then rename so vendors never pick up partial files.
Integration tests against [a containerised OpenSSH server] in CI.
f: Why not just pick one library?
Vendors differ and libraries evolve; the abstraction let us switch per vendor safely (next question has the story).
How do you handle large files?
Stream them without loading into memory, with resumable transfers where supported.
w: I design for change so new requirements don't ripple through callers.

p3-13.q: ComponentPro was the original library, but its updates had slowed and in [2024] a depot vendor disabled older algorithms like ssh-rsa with SHA-1, breaking our connection; SSH.NET was free but we wanted commercial support for a regulated product. I compared all three on modern algorithm support, support and patching, licence cost and behaviour against each vendor's test server, built a Rebex provider behind the existing interface, and we moved vendors to it one at a time by configuration.
i: Algorithm terms worth knowing: rsa-sha2-256/512 host keys, curve25519-sha256 key exchange, aes256-gcm ciphers.
Evaluation matrix made the decision objective and reviewable.
Keeping other providers as fallback reduced risk during migration.
Lesson: abstraction paid off; no caller code changed.
f: Isn't three libraries over-engineering?
Temporarily, for migration and fallback; the plan was to retire ComponentPro once all vendors moved.
What did Rebex cost?
[A commercial licence], justified by support and regulated-product needs.
w: I make technical decisions with clear criteria and evidence.

p3-14.q: I implemented Rebex behind the existing interface with unit tests and integration tests against [a containerised OpenSSH server] in CI (key exchange, host keys, a [500 MB] file, timeouts, reconnects), took it through FV, TechOps and UAT with evidence, then enabled it in production by configuration for [one low-volume vendor] for [two weeks] while watching logs and alerts before switching the rest. No failed transfers were caused by the switch.
i: Canary by configuration: a per-vendor Provider setting, no redeploy needed to switch or roll back.
Observability: transfer success and duration metrics per provider, alerts on failures.
Rollback plan: flip config back to the previous provider.
Same pattern as feature flags: deploy dark, enable gradually.
f: What would make you roll back?
Any failed transfer or auth error attributable to the new provider.
How did you get evidence for GxP?
Test reports from FV and UAT with transfer logs attached to the change record.
w: I release risky changes gradually with a rollback ready.

p3-15.q: Study setup teams typed [300+] site records by hand over [two to three days]. I built a CSV import (up to [5 MB, ~10,000 rows]) that streams with CsvHelper, validates in stages (headers, types, mandatory fields, duplicates in file and database, business rules), shows a preview of every error, then saves all-or-nothing in batches inside one transaction with an audit entry per record and a file hash to block re-imports. It is live in production and a [300-site] setup takes [under an hour].
i: Staged validation fails fast on structural errors before expensive database checks.
Duplicate checks with one set-based query instead of per-row lookups.
Error report downloadable as CSV with row, column and reason.
[Concurrency limit 2 per user] and request size limits protect the system.
Tests: unit test per rule, Playwright end-to-end for upload, preview and confirm.
f: Why InvariantCulture?
So numbers and dates parse the same on every server regardless of locale.
How did you handle a 10,000-row transaction?
Batched inserts inside one transaction with a reasonable timeout; tested at maximum size.
w: I deliver features end to end, from requirements to production.

p3-16.q: In [2024] a manual check caught a study transfer about to overwrite a target study that already had randomized subjects. I replaced the checklist with a backend guard that runs five checks before any transfer: target study status (block if live with subjects or dispensed kits), version compatibility, allowed direction, no transfer already in progress (lock), and user role plus a change request reference; each failure returns a clear reason and every attempt is audited.
i: Fail-closed: if any check can't be evaluated, block.
Lock with sp_getapplock or a unique "transfer in progress" row to prevent races.
Specific error codes help users fix the issue instead of raising tickets.
Released in [2025]; blocked [a handful of] unsafe attempts in its first months.
f: Why check in the backend, not just the UI?
The UI can be bypassed; the API is the real boundary.
Can an admin override it?
[Only with a documented emergency process and dual approval], audited.
w: I turn near-misses into system-enforced safeguards.

p3-17.q: I merge the features committed for the release, resolve conflicts and tag the version across application, APIs, database and UI; build once and produce artifacts; run automated multi-node installs with Ansible, Python and Shell; and promote the same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production, verifying versions, health and smoke tests at each step, with evidence and approvals recorded for the regulated process.
i: Release checklist per team item: status, validation evidence, config changes, DB scripts.
Verification: version endpoint on every node, health checks, key business smoke tests.
Config and database changes reviewed separately (the ValidateOnStart lesson).
Since [2025] the CIRT MCP server runs most steps; humans approve and decide on failures.
f: What's the most common release problem?
Environment configuration differences, which is why we validate options at startup and use checklists.
How do you handle a late feature?
Agree with the product owner to move it to the next release rather than risk validation.
w: I bring order and traceability to complex, multi-team releases.

p3-18.q: In [mid-2024] a RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark during a [large vendor shipment-status file], blocked publishers and dropped connections, and for [about 40 minutes] status updates silently never reached the shipment service. On support, I confirmed it through CloudWatch, Grafana and the management UI, drained the backlog, replayed the missed window from vendor files (safe because consumers upsert), then fixed the root cause with publisher confirms, retries, memory tuning and alerts. All [about 1,200] updates were recovered that evening, with no silent loss since.
i: Root cause vs trigger: the file was the trigger; publishing without confirms was the root cause.
Prevention: confirms with async tracking, alarms on memory, blocked connections and zero incoming rate, consumer scaling on queue depth.
Blameless post-mortem shared with the team.
Code for confirms is in Part 2, Q40.
f: Why didn't anyone notice sooner?
There were no errors to alert on; we added a rate-drop alert.
Did patients get affected?
No; randomization and dispensing were unaffected, only shipment status display was delayed.
w: I stay calm under pressure and restore service first.
I fix causes, not just symptoms, and share lessons.

p3-19.q: I delivered three security fixes in [2024]: real token-based logout (shorter access tokens, refresh-token revocation and a jti denylist in ElastiCache), SSO "request header too long" failures (auth ticket moved to a server-side ITicketStore, cookie from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB]) and reverse tabnabbing ([about 40] links fixed with rel=noopener noreferrer plus an ESLint rule). Each had tests and went through review and the regulated release process.
i: Pattern: fix the root cause and add a guard so it cannot come back (tests, lint rule).
Map to OWASP: broken authentication/session management, security misconfiguration, client-side risks.
Performance impact measured: denylist check about [1 ms] per request.
Detailed stories: Part 2 Q48–50.
f: Which was hardest?
The SSO cookie issue, because it only affected some users and needed a pattern to reproduce.
How do you find security issues proactively?
